blocks.text: Linear Regression covered the genuinely simplest case, one feature predicting one continuous target. Real, practical problems almost always genuinely involve several features at once, square footage, bedrooms, and location all together predicting price, not just one feature considered in isolation. Multiple linear regression extends the exact same core idea directly to that far more common, real case.

This topic covers how the simple regression equation genuinely expands to include every available feature at once, why a coefficient in this multi feature setting means something genuinely different than a simple regression slope, a real, practical danger that emerges specifically once multiple features enter the picture, multicollinearity, and how the underlying computation genuinely generalizes from a single line to a full, multi dimensional hyperplane.
1. From a Line to a Hyperplane

blocks.alt: From a Line to a Hyperplane
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424185-948330455.png

With genuinely many feature dimensions at once, square footage, bedrooms, and location score all feeding into one model, the fitted relationship is genuinely no longer a simple, two dimensional line, it becomes a hyperplane, a flat surface extended across every one of those feature dimensions simultaneously. This is genuinely still a straight, flat relationship in the mathematical sense, simply extended into more dimensions than a single line can show.

This is worth holding onto directly, multiple linear regression is genuinely not a fundamentally different algorithm from simple linear regression, it is the exact same straight line idea, generalized to however many features a real dataset actually provides.
2. Expanding the Equation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424424-197243323.png

The simple regression equation, y equals one weight times x plus an intercept, genuinely expands directly, y now equals every feature weight multiplied by its own feature value, all summed together, plus one shared intercept. Each feature genuinely gets its own dedicated coefficient, learned together with every other coefficient during the exact same training process.

This expanded equation is still genuinely fit the same way as before, minimizing mean squared error across every prediction, just now searching across a genuinely larger number of coefficients simultaneously rather than just one slope and one intercept.
3. A Worked Example
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424425-752883315.png
Fitting scikit-learn LinearRegression on multiple features at once shows this genuine expansion directly, in practice.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import pandas as pd

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": [900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 3, 4, 4],
    "location_score": [3, 5, 4, 8, 7],
})
y = pd.Series([250000, 310000, 360000, 410000, 460000])

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

print("Coefficients:", dict(zip(X.columns, model.coef_)))
print("Intercept:", model.intercept_)

blocks.text: The exact same fit call from the previous topic genuinely now returns three coefficients instead of one, each learned together, simultaneously, in a single training pass across all three features at once.

blocks.text: 4. Interpreting a Coefficient Now Means Something Different

blocks.alt: Interpreting a Coefficient Now Means Something Different
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424425-857022662.png

In simple linear regression, the single slope genuinely captured the entire, full relationship between the one feature and the target. In multiple linear regression, each coefficient genuinely represents the effect of that one feature specifically holding every other feature constant, a real, meaningfully different interpretation, the coefficient on square footage now genuinely answers, how much does price change for one more square foot, assuming bedrooms and location score stay exactly the same.

This distinction genuinely matters in practice, a feature coefficient can even change sign once other features are added to the model, because the other features are now genuinely absorbing some of the relationship that feature alone used to carry entirely by itself.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A coefficient in multiple linear regression genuinely means the effect of that feature holding every other feature constant, not its full, standalone relationship with the target the way a simple regression slope does.

blocks.text: 5. The Real Danger: Multicollinearity
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424425-264865082.png

When two input features are genuinely highly correlated with each other, exactly the redundancy first covered back in Feature Relationships, the model has genuine difficulty telling their individual effects apart, since they move together in the data. This can make individual coefficients genuinely unstable, small changes in the data can swing a coefficient considerably, or even flip its sign, even though the model overall predictions often stay reasonably reliable.

This is exactly why checking for genuine feature to feature redundancy, using the correlation techniques covered back in Feature Selection, matters directly before trusting any single coefficient interpretation in a multiple regression model, the coefficient itself can become genuinely misleading even when the model as a whole still predicts reasonably well.

blocks.text: 6. The Feature Matrix, Now With Many Columns

blocks.alt: The Feature Matrix, Now With Many Columns
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424426-874283347.png

The genuine feature matrix X, first introduced back in Tabular Data, now genuinely holds one column per feature, square footage, bedrooms, and location score all sitting side by side, with each row still genuinely representing one single instance, exactly as covered there. Multiple linear regression is, in a real sense, simply that same matrix used to its full, intended extent.

This connection is worth holding onto directly, the X and y split, and the row as instance, column as feature vocabulary from much earlier in this course, was always building toward genuinely using every available column together, exactly what this topic finally puts into practice.
7. How the Best Fit Hyperplane Actually Gets Found

blocks.alt: How the Best Fit Hyperplane Actually Gets Found
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443424426-304018714.png

The normal equation covered back in Linear Regression genuinely generalizes directly into matrix form, solving for every coefficient at once using matrix operations on the entire feature matrix X and target vector y simultaneously, rather than the single slope and intercept case handled before. This genuinely remains an exact, direct computation, no iteration required, for a genuinely reasonable number of features.

For datasets with a genuinely very large number of features, or ones causing real numerical instability, gradient descent, briefly previewed back in Linear Regression, becomes the more genuinely practical approach, iteratively refining every coefficient together rather than solving for them all directly in one matrix step.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Check feature to feature correlations, using the techniques from Feature Selection, before trusting any individual coefficient in a multiple regression model with many features.

blocks.text: 8. Multiple Linear Regression Versus What Comes Next

This topic extended linear regression to genuinely handle many features at once, still fundamentally fitting a straight, flat relationship, just across more dimensions. Both this topic and the previous one, though, share one real, remaining limitation, they can only capture genuinely straight line relationships, even in this expanded, multi feature form.

The next topic, Polynomial Regression, addresses exactly that limitation directly, capturing genuinely curved relationships while staying within this same core linear regression framework, directly reusing the polynomial features first covered back in Polynomial Features.

items: Multiple linear regression genuinely extends the simple case to many features, fitting a hyperplane rather than a line.
The equation genuinely expands to one weight per feature, all learned together in a single training pass.
A coefficient here genuinely means the effect of that feature holding every other feature constant.
Multicollinearity, genuinely correlated input features, can make individual coefficients unstable.
The feature matrix X, from Tabular Data, is genuinely used to its full, intended extent in this topic.
The next topic, Polynomial Regression, genuinely captures curved relationships within this same linear framework.
